opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I hear that a lot, and I think it's a fair thing to push on. Part of why it happens is that math and coding are where progress is easiest to measure. You have a proof or you don't; the tests pass or they fail. So when we talk publicly about capabilities, those are the domains where we can point to something concrete, and it can sound like that's all the models are good at, or all we care about.

But a big part of my work has been trying to close that gap: building evaluations that look much more like real economically valuable work. Not puzzle problems, but the kinds of tasks people actually do in their jobs, like a legal memo, a financial analysis, a nursing care plan, a sales presentation. We have experienced professionals in those fields write the tasks and grade the outputs, and we compare the model's work to what a human expert would produce. That gives a much more honest picture than a leaderboard number on a competition math set.

And what you see when you do that is a mixed picture. The models are surprisingly strong across a lot of professional domains, often close to expert quality on well-scoped tasks. But they also fail in ways that matter: formatting problems, not following instructions carefully, occasionally making things up, missing context a human would just know. So I'd say the honest answer is that it's neither hype nor dismissal. The capabilities are real and broader than math, but you should measure them on the actual work you care about rather than take anyone's word for it, including ours.

The other thing I'd add is that math and research matter a lot in their own right. If models can meaningfully accelerate scientific discovery, that's a huge deal even if they're still clumsy at some everyday tasks. So I don't think those strengths are "limited" in the sense the critique implies. We just need to be precise about what we're claiming and back it up with evidence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that perception is worth taking seriously, honestly, because there's a real version of it. If you spend your day watching a model crack competition math problems or help with a research proof, it's very easy to extrapolate and say "this thing is basically a scientist now." And then someone asks it to book a flight or fill out a form and it falls over in some embarrassing way, and they reasonably go, "what were you people talking about?"

But I'd push back on the framing a little. Math and research aren't where the strengths happen to be by accident. They're where we can measure most cleanly. There's a right answer, you can grade it, you can run it a thousand times. So that's where progress shows up first and loudest, and it's where we tend to talk about it because we can actually back it up with numbers. That creates a sampling bias in what people hear from us.

The thing I spend a lot of my time on is trying to close that gap. We've put a lot of effort into building evals for messier, more realistic work: can the model complete tasks the way an expert would actually do them on the job, in domains like law or finance or medicine, judged by people in those fields? And what you see is that the picture is more uneven than the math headlines suggest. The models are genuinely strong at some professional tasks and genuinely bad at others, especially anything long-horizon or that requires understanding context nobody wrote down. We try to say that out loud, including the parts where the models don't do well.

So I'd say the critique isn't that we're lying about math. The critique is about generalization claims, and the right response to that isn't to hype less, it's to measure more broadly and be honest about what the measurements show. If the capability is real in a domain, it should show up in an eval that domain experts would recognize as fair. If it doesn't, then we shouldn't be claiming it, and I'd rather be the one who finds that out before someone else does.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a fair question underneath that: when we say a model is better, better for whom, and at what? Math and research are areas where we can measure progress relatively clearly, but those results don’t automatically tell you how useful a model will be in your day-to-day life.

If it can solve a difficult math problem but struggles with the task you actually need help with, that gap matters. We need to be specific about what’s improved, honest about what still doesn’t work, and connect the progress to things people can actually use. Researchers can be excited about a result, but that excitement isn’t a substitute for demonstrating its value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two questions there: how capable are the models, and how well do we communicate what they’re useful for? Math and research give us relatively clear ways to measure progress, but those results don’t automatically tell you how useful a model will be in someone’s day-to-day work.

If a model does well on a difficult benchmark but struggles with something you need it to do, that gap matters. We should be specific about what we’ve demonstrated, where the model still fails, and what remains uncertain. Enthusiasm about progress is understandable, but it needs to come with that specificity.
